section_1.title: The Intuitive Hook: The Prism Analogy
section_1.content: Introduce the Fourier Transform as a prism for signals. Just as a glass prism breaks white light into a rainbow of colors, the Fourier Transform breaks a complex time-domain signal into its constituent sine waves (frequencies).
section_1.example: Visualizing a complex sound wave from a piano chord being separated into its individual notes (frequencies) on a music staff.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Review: Periodic Motion
section_2.content: Briefly define a simple periodic signal using the sine function: f(t) = A sin(ωt + φ). Explain that any signal can be represented as a sum of these simple building blocks.
section_2.example: An animation showing a single rotating vector (phasor) creating a smooth sine wave on a graph.

section_3.title: The Core Concept: From Time to Frequency
section_3.content: Explain the transition from the Time Domain (how a signal changes over time) to the Frequency Domain (how much of each frequency exists in the signal). Emphasize the integral equation: F(ω) = ∫ f(t)e^(-iωt)dt.
section_3.example: An animation of a 'spiky' time-domain signal transforming into a 'bar chart' representation in the frequency domain.

section_4.title: Practical Application: Digital Noise Reduction
section_4.content: Demonstrate how the Fourier Transform allows us to 'isolate' specific frequencies. By converting a noisy audio signal into the frequency domain, we can identify and 'cut' the high-frequency static while keeping the low-frequency human voice.
section_4.example: A recording of a cat meowing in a noisy room; visual representation shows the cat's meow as a distinct frequency spike that is kept, while the 'static' noise is filtered out.

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap: The Fourier Transform is a bridge between time and frequency. It is the fundamental tool for modern data processing, from MP3 compression to medical MRI imaging.
section_5.example: A quick visual montage: A radio receiving a signal, a smartphone compressing a photo, and a brain scan, all linked by the Fourier Transform icon.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
